# Filtering by file type in ripgrep

If you search text for a living, you already know the routine: you only want the
Rust files, or everything *except* the minified JavaScript, or just this one
odd extension your team invented. You can spell that out with globs every time
(`rg 'fn run' -g '*.rs'`), but ripgrep gives you a shorter, named way to say the
same thing. A *type* is just a name assigned to one or more globs. Four flags
manage them: `-t/--type`, `-T/--type-not`, `--type-add`, and `--type-list`.

## `-t/--type`: search only this type

`--type` limits the search to files matching a named type.

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

The two lines are equivalent; the short form takes its value with no space.
Because `rust` bundles the relevant globs, you don't have to remember whether
you want `*.rs` alone or something broader. The C type covers both source and
headers, so `rg 'int main' -tc` searches `*.c` and `*.h` at once.

You can repeat the flag. `rg -trust -tpython` searches both Rust and Python
files. Note that `--type` has lower precedence than the `-g/--glob` flag and
than any rules found in ignore files, so a `.gitignore` entry or an explicit
glob still wins.

## `-T/--type-not`: search everything but this type

`--type-not` is the mirror image. Where `-t` means "include files of this
type", `-T` means "exclude files of this type."

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

You can repeat it, and you can mix the two on one command line. `rg -Trust
-ttoml -Tjson` reads left to right, so each flag adds to the running set of
inclusions and exclusions.

## The special `all` type

Both `--type` and `--type-not` accept the special value `all`.

`--type all` behaves as if you had passed `--type` for every type ripgrep
knows, including any you added on the command line. The effect is a "whitelist"
search: ripgrep only searches files it *recognizes* through its type
definitions, and skips anything with an unknown extension.

`--type-not all` is the inverse "blacklist" search: ripgrep only searches files
that are *unrecognized*. This is worth a moment of thought, because recognition
hinges on the globs, not on what the file really is. Suppose you have a shell
script named `my-shell-script` (no extension) that sources
`my-shell-library.bash`. Both `rg --type sh` and `rg --type all` search only
`my-shell-library.bash`, because the `sh` globs don't match an extensionless
name. Conversely, `rg --type-not all` searches `my-shell-script` but not
`my-shell-library.bash`.

## `--type-add`: define your own type

ripgrep ships with a large set of predefined types for well-known public
formats. When those don't cover your work, define your own. Say you often
search "web" files — JavaScript, HTML, and CSS:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

The syntax is `name:glob`. Only one glob per flag, so repeat `--type-add` to
add more — or fold them into a single brace glob:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

That defines `web` as `*.{html,css,js}`, then searches for `title` in matching
files. Unless you also pass `--type-clear`, added globs join any globs already
defined for that name rather than replacing them. Type names must consist only
of Unicode letters or numbers; punctuation isn't allowed.

You can also build a type out of existing types with the `include` directive.
It takes one or more already-defined type names, comma-separated, and imports
their globs:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md'
```

That makes `src` match C++, Python, and Markdown files. You can keep adding
plain globs to it afterward:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo'
```

One caveat worth stressing: `--type-add` applies only to the current command.
It is not saved anywhere. To make a type available every time, either alias
ripgrep —

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

— or put `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` in your configuration file.

## `--type-list`: see what's defined

To review the types, run `--type-list`. Each type prints on its own line,
followed by a `:` and a comma-delimited list of its globs:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

The listing accounts for any `--type-add` and `--type-clear` flags on the same
command, so a type you define appears in the output even though it isn't one of
ripgrep's built-ins. That makes `--type-list` the quickest way to confirm a
custom definition matches what you meant before you rely on it.
